statements.text: Under a care perspective, responding to the more urgent threat to life normally has priority over an earlier but weaker relational assurance when the difference in vulnerability is significant.
Keeping a promise is an important element of sustaining trust within caring relationships.
Ellis has stronger reason of care to give the blanket to Rowan.
Breaking the promise to Sasha is a morally relevant harm that counts against giving the blanket to Rowan.

supports.explanation: Higher expected survival for Rowan makes need more urgent under n1
n2 applies to show moral cost of promise-breaking

reasons.value: Higher chance of saving a life (80% vs 60%) and responding to greatest vulnerability
Ellis keeps the promise made to Sasha, sustaining a trust relationship

comparisons.explanation: Action A has a higher expected survival benefit and responds to the more serious vulnerability, which under n1 outweighs the relational cost captured in R2.

conclusion: Caring responsiveness to the most acute life-threatening need provisionally supports giving the blanket to Rowan, though the moral cost of breaking Ellis’s promise to Sasha remains a live concern.
strongest_objection: Breaking Ellis’s explicit promise to Sasha undermines trust and may inflict relational harm that care ethics takes seriously.
answer_to_objection: The care duty to address the gravest vulnerability (80% chance to save Rowan versus 60% for Sasha) is, in this context, more urgent than fulfilling the earlier assurance; responsiveness to life-or-death need can override but does not erase the wrong of breaking a promise.
reversal_condition: If the survival probabilities were roughly equal, or Sasha’s need became at least as urgent as Rowan’s, the relational promise could tip the balance toward giving the blanket to Sasha.
residual_disagreement: Whether Ellis could have competently avoided promising before full knowledge and whether the lingering harm to caring relationships outweighs the 20-percentage-point survival difference
